extracted.intended_audience: general readers and folklorists interested in Cornish folk customs, charms, and traditional rites
extracted.subtask_description: Recording and describing traditional Cornish rituals, charms, divination practices, and wedding/folk customs, including exact procedural steps, incantations, prohibitions, and local interpretations. Useful for folklorists, local historians, or readers collecting vernacular ritual practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imprecatory power of Psalm 109
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading or reciting the 109th Psalm (especially imprecatory portions) shortly before death is believed to invoke a curse; the reciter may pronounce doom on others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual example: the hanged seaman repeated portions of Psalm 109 and uttered that Sir Cloudesley Shovel and those who saw him hanged 'should never reach the land alive.' Local tradition attributes the wreck of the 'Association' to that recitation. Use as causal explanation/omen in local narrative; regarded as dangerous to recite such imprecations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Madron Well healing ritual (procedure and signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Curing ritual at Madron Well: strip the child 'as naked as it was born'; plunge it three times 'against the sun'; pass the creature quickly nine times around the spring, going from east to west (with the sun); dress and lay the child near the water; if it sleeps and 'plenty of bubbles rise in the well' it is a good sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The full practice includes leaving a piece 'rented, not cut' from the child's (or user's) clothing near the well (between stones or hung on a thorn) as an offering. The attendant (e.g. 'An' Katty') directs rites and is customarily paid in goods (yarn) rather than money. The ritual is only effective when the spring is 'working' (rising strongly). If any word is spoken near the water during dipping, 'they had to come again.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence prohibition during well rites
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There musn't be a word spoken all the time they are near the water, it would spoil the spell.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speaking while the dipping/ritual is in progress is explicitly considered to nullify the cure and requires repetition of the ceremony. This is a strict behavioral rule attached to well-ritual efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offering of a rented (not cut) piece of clothing
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece 'rented, not cut' from the child's clothes or from that of anybody using the well must be left near the well for good luck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement: out of sight between stones bordering the brooklet or hung on a thorn by the chapel wall. Size may be 'ever so small a bit.' This is the customary non-monetary payment/pledge associated with the rite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divination at Madron Well (pins, pebbles, and bubbles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divination by dropping pins or pebbles into the well: think of persons when dropping objects and interpret whether the objects remain together or separate as the couple's fate; the number of bubbles rising in the water when stamped near the well may 'mark the years' in answer to questions of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only attempted when the spring is 'working.' Often no names are spoken—thinking of the person suffices. This is treated as a social pastime among maidens as well as a divinatory practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Men-an-tol (Crick-stone) crawling ritual
rubrics_metrics.description: Crawl ('crame') nine times through the hole in the centre stone, going 'against the sun's course', for the cure of lumbago, sciatica, and other back 'cricks'; young children were also put through it to ensure healthy growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a fixed count (nine times) and a specified direction (against the sun). The stones are also compared to other holed stones (Tolmen) used similarly for curing. Antiquarian interpretations (sepulchral vs astronomical functions) are noted but do not alter the ritual prescription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sun-course rule for rituals and household tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: General rule: 'going against the sun will backen a disease but in all other cases the sun's course must be followed.' Examples: do not unream (skim) milk or stir cream against the sun's course; specific healing rites sometimes require going against the sun, otherwise follow sun's direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prescriptive cosmology governs many practices: when to go with vs against the sun is considered essential to efficacy or luck. Local informants cite wide application to dairy work, healing rites, and charms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wedding-night 'tanning'/'beating to bed' ritual (ensure luck and fertility)
rubrics_metrics.description: On returning to the bridal-chamber, guests 'beat them in bed, with stockings, straps, braces, or anything they could lay hands on'—a rough treatment believed to ensure happiness and 'the heritage and gift ... of a numerous family.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performed by the assembled guests until elders deem it time to stop (example: leader says 'Les go back ... it's nearly twelve o'clock'). A traditional justification is that failure to perform this would bring bad luck to the couple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stocking-throwing to predict first-born sex
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern/less violent variant: guests throw stockings (weighted with stones) at the bride and bridegroom in bed; the first one to hit of the happy couple 'betokens the sex of their first-born.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A divinatory game replacing the older rougher custom; implementation detail: weight stockings to make them effective projectiles. Interpreted as omen/forecast rather than healing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charm for scald/wild-fire/burns (procedure and words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure: gather nine bramble leaves into a vessel of spring water; pass each leaf over the diseased part while repeating three times to each leaf: 'Three ladies come from the east, One with fire and two with frost; Out with thee fire, and in with thee frost, In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.' Then take a stick of fire from the hearth and pass it over and around the diseased part while repeating the above nine times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counts (nine leaves; three repetitions per leaf; nine passes of the fire-stick) and the exact prayer-like formula are required. The ritual mixes vegetal, water, verbal, and sympathetic-fire elements; the precise words are part of the cure's authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charm for thorn-prick, boils, 'kennels'
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal formula: 'Christ was crowned with thorns, The thorns did bleed but did not rot, No more shall thy finger (_or whatever part it may be_), In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The charmer typically passes the leaf or touches/places the thumb on the diseased part (thumb-placement rule applies to most charms except the first listed). The incantation evokes Christ's thorn-crown as symptomatic authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charm for staunching blood
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal formula: 'Christ was born in Bethlehem, Baptised in the river Jordan; There he digg'd a well. And turn'd the water against the hill, So shall thy blood stand still. In the name, &c.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spoken while manipulating water or making accompanying passes; intended as an immediate-stop bleeding charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charm series for 'tetter' (skin complaint)
rubrics_metrics.description: A counting/iteration charm: e.g. 'Tetter, tetter, thou hast nine sisters. God bless the flesh and preserve the bone, Perish thou tetter and be thou gone, In the name, &c.' and then repeated reducing the sister-count (eight, seven,... until 'thou hast no sister').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continue the charm decrementally until the final 'no sister' verse. The numeric countdown is an explicit procedural element of the cure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charm for toothache
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal formula: 'Christ pass'd by his brother's door, Saw his brother lying on the floor. 'What aileth thee, brother? Pain in thy teeth? Thy teeth shall pain thee no more.' In the name, &c.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The charmer places his or her thumb on the diseased part in all but the first charm (i.e., thumb-placement is customary here). Oral recitation and touch combine for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orality rule: charms must not be written
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If written they are useless, and the giver of a written one thenceforth loses the power to cure by charming.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charms are transmitted orally only; writing or giving a written charm is explicitly stated to destroy the charm's efficacy and the charmer's future power. This is a transmission/ownership rule governing practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bible-and-key divination (sortilege)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divination by letting a Bible fall open and taking the 'first words the eye may glance on' as an answer to a doubt; also divination with a Bible and key.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common English practice noted here as present locally; no fixed verbal formula beyond interpreting the first-glanced words. Treated as a form of sortilege or bibliomancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offerings to local guardian spirits (Bucka)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fishermen (e.g. Newlyn and Mousehal) used to leave a portion of their catch on the sand at night for Bucka (a local spirit) as an offering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice is described as customary to propitiate a local spirit; it forms part of ritualized dealings with benevolent/ambiguous local powers and may inform local nicknames ('Newlyn Buckas').
